thread.title: Are Recalls Really Up 400 Percent? Recall Counts Held Flat While Recalled Units Jumped More Than Fourfold, Mostly in Drugs and Devices - NewsBreak
thread.title_full: Are Recalls Really Up 400 Percent? Recall Counts Held Flat While Recalled Units Jumped More Than Fourfold, Mostly in Drugs and Devices - NewsBreak

author: Chloe Parker
title: Are Recalls Really Up 400 Percent? Recall Counts Held Flat While Recalled Units Jumped More Than Fourfold, Mostly in Drugs and Devices - NewsBreak
text:
By Chloe Parker ,
1 hours ago Joe Raedle | Getty Images A claim that U.S. recalls are up 400 percent this year spread widely on social media after a summer of outbreaks . The figure traces back to a real number, but not the one many shoppers assumed. The number of recalls barely changed in the first half of 2026. What jumped was the number of units recalled, and most of that jump came from medicines and medical devices, not groceries.
The underlying data comes from the Sedgwick Product Safety and Recall Index , published Aug. 20 by Sedgwick, a claims management company that also sells product recall services. It found regulators recorded 1,634 recalls in the first half of 2026, compared with 1,636 in the same period of 2025. Recalled units rose 345.5 percent, from 211.2 million to 941.2 million, which is about four and a half times the earlier total.
For shoppers, the distinction matters. A larger number of units can come from a few very large recalls, and it says little about whether any given grocery trip is riskier. Food recall counts this year are actually running lower than last year by one independent tally.
Where the 400 Percent Came From Roger Hancock, chief executive of Recall InfoLink, wrote in a Food Safety News opinion column that the 400 percent figure spread through a social media creator who said she had read it somewhere without citing a source. He tied it to the Sedgwick unit numbers. Recall InfoLink also sells recall communication services, so its CEO has a business interest in how recalls are discussed.
Sedgwick's own release does not use 400 percent. Its figure is a 345.5 percent increase in units, which means recalled units roughly quadrupled. The release covers recalls across autos, consumer products, food and drink, pharmaceuticals and medical devices, not food alone.
That breadth is the key detail. Pharmaceutical units recalled rose 914 percent to 471.6 million, and medical device units rose 516.8 percent to 313.1 million, according to Sedgwick. Together those two categories account for about 785 million of the 941.2 million units, or roughly 83 percent, based on Sedgwick's figures.
The Food Numbers Tell a Mixed Story Food does show a large increase on one measure. Sedgwick reported that USDA food recalls by volume climbed 2,432.1 percent to 37.2 million pounds, the third-highest level in more than 15 years. USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service covers meat, poultry and some egg products, so that figure does not include most packaged foods, produce or dairy.
A few very large recalls can drive that kind of jump. Recall Bench , an independent site that compiles official FDA and USDA recall data, lists a USDA recall by Ajinomoto Foods North America from February and March 2026 at 6,037,289 pounds, the second-largest by weight in its records since 2014.
Counting recall events instead gives a different picture. Recall Bench reports 420 combined FDA food enforcement events and USDA recalls or public health alerts from Jan. 1 through Oct. 7, 2026, which it says is 11 percent lower than the same dates last year. Of those, 167 were Class I, the most serious category. The site says counts can rise as agencies post late entries, and it is not affiliated with any government agency.
Sedgwick also said that, with July data included, U.S. recalls have now passed one billion units for the year, only the fourth time that has happened in the past 15 years. That total again spans every product category it tracks.
Different sources count different things, which is why recall numbers often seem to conflict. FDA enforcement events, company announcements, individual product entries and fiscal versus calendar years can all produce different totals for the same period.
Size, Not Frequency, Is the Industry Concern Both Sedgwick and Hancock argue the real shift is scale. "Businesses cannot mistake stable event totals for stable exposure risk," said Chris Harvey, a senior vice president at Sedgwick, in the company's release. When one supplier serves many brands, a single contamination problem can reach many products and states at once.
This summer's Cyclospora outbreak linked to iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms de Mexico shows how that works. The recalled lettuce reached Taco Bell restaurants and grocery products, and the outbreak grew to 12,883 confirmed illnesses in 21 states, according to FDA's final update. Large, shared supply chains can make one problem look like many.
Hancock argued that bigger recalls point toward a need for faster tracing and clearer consumer notices. "A large recall doesn't automatically mean the food supply is unsafe," he wrote.
Advice for Shoppers Reading Recall Headlines The practical message is to respond to specific recalls, not headline percentages. A recall applies to particular products, lot codes, and dates. Checking the official notice and matching the code on the package is more useful than avoiding a whole category of food.
Official notices are posted by FDA for most foods and by USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service for meat, poultry and some egg products. Each notice lists the product names, package sizes, codes, and states involved.
Large recalls also mean affected products can turn up under many brand names. When a recall involves a shared ingredient, such as peppers, lettuce or a seasoning, it is worth checking store-brand and prepared items as well as the named brand.
Sedgwick publishes its index quarterly, so third-quarter figures should show whether the unit surge continued. Food World News will report the next release and continue to cover individual recalls with the product details shoppers need.
What People Are Asking Are food recalls up 400 percent? No. The figure traces to recalled units across all product types. Recall counts were flat, and one tally shows food recall events down 11 percent this year.
What does the data actually show? Sedgwick counted 1,634 recalls in the first half of 2026 versus 1,636 a year earlier, while recalled units rose 345.5 percent to 941.2 million.
What drove the jump in units? Mostly pharmaceuticals, at 471.6 million units, and medical devices, at 313.1 million.
Did food recalls grow at all? USDA meat and poultry recalls rose to 37.2 million pounds, driven partly by a few very large recalls.
Who produced these numbers? Sedgwick, a claims and recall services company. Recall Bench, an independent site, compiles official FDA and USDA data.
How should I respond to a recall? Check the official notice, match the lot code and date on your package, and follow the instructions to discard or return it.
